absent: Timer, protected hypervisor and nested VGIC helpers invoked during put and load are not routed here, so their contracts and ordering effects beyond the call sites cannot be determined.

Exact numeric values, bit widths and field positions for VMID mask, generation base, index space size, list register state and hardware flags, and VGIC control fields are not present in these fragments.
Full definitions and ownership or locking rules for vCPU, distributor, interrupt descriptor and virtual processing element structures are not shown.
Distributor initialization, affinity failure recovery beyond error propagation, and doorbell semantics on current revisions are not specified by these fragments.
Hypervisor trap configuration values, host context layout, and fixed mapping allocation policy are not visible here.
Scheduling flag lifecycle and the complete low power and nested exception state machines are only partially observable.

findings.text: Host vCPU teardown exposes a top level put routine plus specialized helpers for debug, floating point, VHE trap and sysreg restoration, nested translation and control release, performance monitor restoration, and interrupt controller release across GIC versions. The fragments show these as externally reachable operations used when leaving guest context.

VMID management and virtual GIC load expose activation and residency operations. One operation ensures the calling CPU holds a current generation VMID for the VM, while the GIC operations make a virtual CPU interface or virtual processing element resident on the current physical CPU.

Top level vCPU put runs protected mode handling first when enabled, saving interrupt state through the hypervisor and marking host state dirty for non protected guests, then invokes debug, floating point, VHE, timer, interrupt controller and host monitor steps in order, releases nested translation state when nested virtualization is present, clears the active VMID marker, detaches the vCPU from its CPU, and performs unsupported CPU cleanup.

Nested shadow creation builds a compact host facing view of guest interrupt state. Control and priority configuration are copied from virtual interface registers into shadow control fields, the enable value is taken from the host copy, and list registers are rebuilt separately so only entries carrying state are retained.

Shadow interrupt state pairs a CPU interface image holding control, virtual machine control, enable, priority mask arrays, list register array and used count with a per CPU wrapper that adds a source index occupancy mask. The per CPU accessor returns the current CPU copy, and the list image is linked to its wrapper through container membership.

Shadow list construction starts with an empty occupancy mask, scans all implemented list positions, skips entries without state, translates the survivors, appends them densely in scan order, records each source position in the mask, and finally sets the used count to the population of the mask.

List entries without a hardware association pass through unchanged. Entries claiming hardware have their virtual interrupt looked up; when the lookup fails or the target is not a hardware backed shared peripheral the hardware claim is dropped, while valid or invalid lookups still rewrite the physical identifier field to the backing hardware value before releasing the reference.

List and priority mask register selectors form contiguous sequences where the selected index is added to the zero based base selector. This yields indexed access to list positions and to the two priority groups without further encoding.

VMID index conversion masks off generation bits to obtain an allocation index, and the reverse conversion applies the same masking so the two helpers are inverses over the index space. Generation match compares the stored and global generations above the index width.

A VM identifier combines a global generation with an allocation index. Activation succeeds immediately when the stored generation is current and the per CPU active slot can be exchanged. Otherwise a fresh value is allocated under lock and published as active. Allocation reuses the prior index when free and honors reserved entries, otherwise takes the next free index, and on exhaustion advances the generation, rebuilds the map from live and reserved values, broadcasts context invalidation, and allocates from the renewed space.

The slow VMID path serializes generation checks, bitmap updates, cursor movement, rollover and publication under a CPU wide spin lock held with interrupts saved. The fast path uses only atomic reads and a relaxed compare exchange on the per CPU active slot and takes no lock.

Direct interrupt load is a no operation when the VM lacks direct support, when the virtual processing element is already resident, or when the vCPU waits in low power state. Otherwise it routes the doorbell to the current CPU, requests residency with the distributor enabled state, and on older controller revisions explicitly clears any lingering pending doorbell before reporting status.

Version five load is idempotent on a residency flag so a second invocation on the low power exit path does nothing. The first invocation restores virtual machine control and priority state through the hypervisor and then marks the element resident.

Interrupt controller put dispatches on the configured distributor model to version specific release, with version two selecting between version three and version two handling according to CPU interface capability. When there is no in kernel chip or no initialization, only trap deactivation is attempted on capable VHE hosts; an unknown model is treated as a fatal programming error.

VHE put first deactivates traps with interrupts masked and then saves guest system state while restoring host user state, clears the sysregs on CPU marker, and clears the hypervisor running vCPU pointer so no guest remains associated with the physical CPU.

Common trap deactivation clears the system trap register, restores the host performance user enable value and clears its on CPU marker when performance monitoring exists, restores the extended hypervisor control when present, and delegates fine grained trap, interrupt controller trap and memory partitioning restoration to dedicated helpers.

Fine grained trap restoration is skipped entirely without the architecture capability, otherwise it writes back host copies for read, write, instruction and debug groups, plus activity monitor controls when present, and for the second generation capability also writes back the second group of controls. Interrupt controller fine grained controls are restored only when the version five CPU interface capability is present.

Memory partitioning trap restoration does nothing without support, otherwise it clears trap and identifier bits while enabling the supervisor control and, when the hypervisor control variant exists, installs host partitioning flags.

Guest EL1 save captures control, translation, fault, timer and linkage state into the CPU context image. Translation extension, permission indirection, overlay, tagging, secondary control and nested hypervisor fields are captured only when the context advertises the corresponding feature or nested mode.

Virtual EL2 save records common fault and configuration state into EL2 slots and, when the E2H view is active, also records control and translation state from EL1 views into EL2 images, with special merging of counter timer bits that differ between revisions. Linkage and optional secondary control are handled in the same pass.

Thirty two bit guest save applies only to guests in thirty two bit EL1 mode and preserves banked status registers plus fault and debug controls, with the debug control preserved only on VHE hosts or when debug registers are in use.

Debug put restores the host debug control on VHE hosts and otherwise acts only for guests with single step enabled, where it records whether host single step was active and adjusts the guest status single step bit according to whether guest single step completion remains pending.

Floating point put returns immediately during nested return or nested exception handling after asserting the host does not own the registers. Otherwise it masks interrupts and, when the guest owns the registers, saves and flushes vector state so later host SIMD use does not observe stale guest data.

Trap deactivation and floating point flushing mask local interrupts around the critical section and restore the prior mask afterward, preventing concurrent guest state changes on the same CPU during the save.

Nested translation put always releases any per CPU virtual control mapping, retains the stage two reference when the vCPU merely scheduled out outside low power wait as a reuse hint, and otherwise drops the reference when it refers to a nested table and clears the active handle.

Virtual control unmapping races a concurrent broadcast invalidation by atomically exchanging the owning CPU to none and clearing the corresponding fixed mapping on the previous owner, with the caller also clearing its local mapping when it lost the race. The reset path requires a non hypervisor context when a mapping is present and always clears the mapped marker.
Host performance monitor restoration runs only when both the performance extension and VHE are present, enabling host events and disabling guest events according to the current event masks.

Version three trap deactivation restores system register enable state when version two compatibility exists, ordering enablement before guest enable when the CPU interface disabled it, and disables the virtual interface control when fine grained trapping was active, when a virtual processing element is attached, or when system register access was disabled.

Version two put captures the active priority mask from the virtual control aperture. Version three put diverts to a nested handler when nested state is present, otherwise saves priority state through the hypervisor on non protected hosts, checks direct interrupt release, and deactivates traps on VHE hosts.
